item.title: Comparing magic state cultivation methods using matrix product states
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — For d=5 regular surface-code fold-transversal cultivation, $|T angle$ logical error rates match $|S angle$ Clifford proxy error rates across the tested noise range. A rotated surface-code scheme achieves ∼1.3× lower expected space-time cost while reaching 10−9 logical error rate.

Grade 0.483 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Tom Hartweg, Asier Piñeiro Orioli

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical depolarising error rate p for d=3 and d=5 magic state cultivation schemes comparing |S⟩ (Stim Clifford proxy) and |T⟩ (exact CAMPS simulation) outputs.

Asks

What is the exact non-Clifford performance and logical error rate of fold-transversal magic state cultivation schemes on surface codes?

Before

Color-code cultivation (Gidney et al.) showed a 7× to 30× higher logical error rate for |T⟩ state cultivation compared to the |S⟩ Clifford proxy.

But

Depolarising SD6 circuit noise model, post-selection on all syndrome detectors and final noiseless decoding, classical simulation on commodity CPU.

Tools

matrix-product states (MPS) · Clifford-augmented MPS (CAMPS) · Pauli pre-screening · subset sampling · Stim

Abstract

Magic state cultivation prepares high-fidelity magic states at low expected space-time costs; however, the exact performance of some schemes is unsettled due to the difficulty in simulating non-Clifford circuits. Here, we use matrix-product states (MPS) based methods to compute the exact performance of two types of fold-transversal cultivation schemes: (i) the Sahay et al method based on the regular surface code S gate, and (ii) a method we propose based on a partially fault-tolerant fold-transversal S gate. We show that for the former protocol at d=5, the |T⟩ output reaches similar logical error rates to the |S⟩ output, traditionally used as a cheap full Clifford proxy. This contrasts with the ∼10× discrepancy reported for the d=5 colour-code scheme of Gidney et al. We also find that our new d=5 scheme has ∼1.3× lower expected space-time cost while still reaching 10⁻⁹ logical error rate. We show that MPS and Clifford-augmented MPS (CAMPS) perform on par with or even better than the recently introduced near-Clifford simulator Clifft on the hardest d=5 regular surface code scheme. Additionally, to speed up simulation, we propose a new pre-screening method based on simple Pauli propagation, lowering by up to three orders of magnitude the required number of exact simulations, and use several simulator-agnostic sampling methods such as subset sampling.

item.title: Exact logical error rates for magic state cultivation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Exact logical error rates for magic state cultivation computed without Monte Carlo sampling; PL(5)(p=10−3)=3.32842537⋯×10−9 with series expansion PL(5)(x)=574375x3+972959741810000x4+O(x5) for x=p/(1−p).

Grade 0.469 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Kwok Ho Wan, Ainhoa Zapirain

Figure

Logical error rate (left), acceptance probability (middle), and truncated series relative error (right) for d=5 cultivation as functions of noise strength p. The analytical curves agree with published Monte Carlo sampling intervals from Clifft and SOFT.

Asks

What are the exact post-selected logical error rates and acceptance probabilities of magic state cultivation circuits across all fault orders using actual T gates instead of sampling with S-gate proxies?

But

Standard uniform circuit-level depolarising noise at parameter p. Excludes escape, grafting, and decoding stages; logical readout is assumed noiseless.

Tools

Pauli propagation · binary tensor network contraction · Chinese remainder theorem over modular primes · exact polynomial series expansion in x=p/(1-p)

Abstract

We compute exactly the acceptance and logical error rates for the distance d=3 and d=5 magic state cultivation circuits from Clifft [arXiv:2604.27058] and SOFT [arXiv:2512.23037] using Pauli propagation and binary tensor contraction. Actual T gates are studied, not the S-gate proxy used for sampling. The calculation includes every fault order at several circuit-level noise strengths (p). We provide a series expansion form to the logical error rates, through order (p/(1-p))¹⁰. The analytical results recover the numerical values from Clifft and SOFT at both d=3 and d=5 to within their sampling uncertainty. Then, we show that the d=3 and d=5 circuits actually have fault distances of d_fault=2 and d_fault=3 respectively, explaining the similar distance degrading effects from the companion code of [Quantum 10, 2134 (2026)].

item.title: Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Flagged double-check circuits eliminate malignant hook errors in magic state cultivation, suppressing pre-escape logical error rate from 𝒪(p3) to 𝒪(p5) and achieving a 4.9× error rate improvement at p=10−3 for a 1.36× attempt overhead.

Grade 0.464 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Tim Chan, Armands Strikis, Zhu Sun, Zhenyu Cai

Asks

Why does T-state cultivation suffer higher logical error rates and lower fault distances than S-state cultivation under circuit-level noise, and how can the full fault distance be restored?

Before

Unflagged distance-3 (distance-5) T-state cultivation degraded to fault distance 2 (fault distance 3), while S-state cultivation retained full fault distance 3 (fault distance 5).

But

Evaluated under standard circuit-level depolarising noise at error rate p=10−3; applies to fixed logical-qubit count with physical qubit count n.

Tools

circuit-level depolarising noise simulations · analytic propagation of Pauli hook errors into coherent Clifford errors · O(n³)-time Clifford acceptance probability algorithm · flagged verification circuits

Abstract

T-state cultivation is a resource-efficient protocol producing logical T states but recent benchmarks show that its logical error rate is considerably higher than intended i.e. than S-state cultivation, which is the analogous protocol for producing logical S states. In this paper, we explain this T-S discrepancy by analytically showing, under circuit-level depolarising noise, that distance-3 (-5) T-state cultivation has fault distance 2 (3) due to Pauli hook errors that propagate to coherent Clifford errors after its final double-check circuit; such errors remain Pauli in S-state cultivation, which consequently retains fault distance 3 (5). As part of our analysis we derive a general formula, and an O(n³)-time algorithm for fixed logical-qubit count, for the acceptance probability of a logical mixed state afflicted with a Clifford error, where n is the physical qubit count. We then design flags that detect the malignant hook errors in cultivation, improving the pre-escape logical error rate from O(p³) to O(p⁵). At noise level p =10⁻³, this is a 4.9× improvement, costing a 1.36× increase in attempts per accepted shot.

item.title: Algorithmic Design of Heralded Linear Optical Circuits for Multipartite Entanglement
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Linear quantum graph framework automates design of heralded linear optical circuits for multipartite entangled states, producing an N=4 cluster state circuit with 26 beam splitters (10 initial photons).

Grade 0.393 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Jaehee Kim, Hon Wai Lau, William J. Munro, Joonsuk Huh, Seungbeom Chin

Figure

Heralded linear optical circuit schematic for generating the 4-qubit cluster state using two ancilla panels, four system panels, and six photon-subtraction detection panels.

Asks

How can heralded linear optical circuits for arbitrary multipartite entangled quantum states be designed systematically rather than via state-specific manual trial and error?

Before

Generating an N=4 cluster state required 45 beam splitters with 9 photons at a success probability of 2.05×10−3 (Banchi et al. 2024 / Ref. [16]).

But

Unweighted initial graph search; ideal photon-number-resolving detectors; computational scaling grows exponentially with ancilla mode count M.

Tools

effective perfect matching (EPM) bipartite graphs · linear quantum graph (LQG) translation rules · graph canonization · reduced density matrix spectral signature matching

Abstract

Heralded multipartite entanglement is a key resource for various quantum information tasks. However, designing linear optical circuits that generate specific target states is generally challenging due to the complexity of the required optical structures. Here we formulate the design of heralded photonic circuits as an algorithmic graph-search problem. Our framework enables the automated construction and optimization of heralded photonic circuits by substantially reducing the search space using the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture. Our strategy reconstructs circuit structures as graphs in the picture and identifies suitable graphs automatically. As a result, we design efficient schemes for a broad range of useful multipartite resource states, including hypergraph magic states, quantum error correcting codes, general three-qubit states and length-1 caterpillar graph states. Our work establishes an algorithmic framework for the systematic discovery of heralded resource states, laying the foundation for the automated design of increasingly complex multipartite entangled resources.

item.title: Quantum Encodings, Private Messages, and Communication Complexity
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Proves equivalence between quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE) and quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM). Every n-to-m-qubit channel has an m-qubit quantum communication QPSM with exponential entanglement, while with ≤cn pre-shared entanglement, communication is bounded by Ω(n).

Grade 0.376 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Asymptotically good Quantum and locally testable classical LDPC codes” · Tom Gur, Miryam Mi-Ying Huang, Er-Cheng Tang

Figure

Schematic of the Pauli-Port Complementarity protocol showing non-interactive local teleportation using pre-shared entanglement before quantum and classical messages are forwarded to the referee.

Asks

Is the linear dependence of quantum randomized encoding size on circuit size inherent, or can it be characterized more tightly via pre-shared entanglement and communication complexity?

Before

Prior QDRE constructions scaled encoding size linearly with circuit size |Q|.

But

Small quantum communication protocols for general channels require pre-shared entanglement exponential in n. Bounded linear entanglement yields an unavoidable worst-case Ω(n) communication/encoding lower bound.

Tools

quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM) · Pauli mixing · port-teleportation · distributed inner product estimation (DIPE) reductions

Abstract

We study the complexity of quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE). We establish a bi-directional connection between the QDRE model and the communication complexity model of quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM), where classical communication is free, and quantum communication is the primary complexity measure. We show the following upper and lower bounds. (1) For every quantum channel mapping n to m qubits, we give a QPSM protocol with quantum communication m, using exponential pre-shared entanglement. In particular, constant-output channels have O(1) quantum communication, and classical-output channels require no quantum communication. (2) With O(n) pre-shared entanglement, every one-qubit-output channel has an O(n)-quantum-communication QPSM protocol. Conversely, there exists a channel and a constant c>0 for which any protocol with at most cn pre-shared entanglement requires Ω(n) quantum communication. (3) In contrast, we identify a structured class of quantum channels, Clifford-induced channels, for which there exist QPSM protocols with O(n) pre-shared entangled qubits and only O(1) quantum communication complexity. Through our connection, we obtain analogous upper and lower bounds on the quantum encoding size of QDRE. Our results show that the amount of pre-shared entanglement plays a central role in quantum encoding size and quantum communication complexity.

item.title: Optical Quantum Computing
item.description:
Worth a look review — Surveys discrete- and continuous-variable optical quantum computing architectures, measurement-based cluster-state models, and non-universal algorithms (boson sampling, VQEs, QML).

Grade 0.371 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Hamza Hasnaoui, Leonardo Limongi, Taira Giordani, Beatrice Polacchi, Alberto Quaranta, Martino Bernard, Fabio Sciarrino, Mirko Lobino

Figure

Taxonomy mapping discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal optical quantum computing models alongside non-universal photonic applications.

Asks

How do optical encoding schemes and computing architectures compare across universal and non-universal quantum platforms?

But

Photonic scaling is constrained by weak single-photon nonlinearities, probabilistic gate generation, and optical propagation losses.

Tools

integrated photonics · continuous-variable squeeze states · discrete-variable cluster states · linear optical interferometry

Abstract

Under the label of optical quantum computing, there are a variety of protocols and experiments that use the quantum properties of light to achieve a computational advantage over classical computing machines. In this review, we describe some of the main implementations, which differ in the type of encoding and in how the computation is performed, whether using gates or cluster states. For each protocol, we describe advantages and challenges with an overview of the experimental results obtained, summarized in tables. Because of the great relevance achieved in this field, there is a section dedicated to non-universal quantum computation with photons, where boson sampling, variational quantum eigensolvers, and quantum machine learning applications are described. The aim is to give the reader the broadest overview of the applications where photons and their quantum properties play a key role in computation.

item.title: Query-Optimal and Gate-Efficient Lindbladian Simulation
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Approximates Lindbladian evolution to diamond-norm error ε using O(τ+log⁡(1/ε)log⁡(e+log⁡(1/ε)/τ)) oracle queries for τ=(αH+αB2)t, matching the Hamiltonian simulation lower bound.

Grade 0.367 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Boyang Chen, Minbo Gao, Xinzhao Wang, Shuo Zhou

Figure

Figure 1: One query followed by G implements Wδ and restores γψ . Here h,z,b are the three components of the private input to G . Blue connections show M⊗I𝖲 acting as in ( 51 ); the other connections implement the projections, swaps, and phases in the explicit action of G in ( 53 ).

Asks

What is the optimal query complexity of simulating Lindbladian dynamics as a function of evolution time and target precision?

Before

Was O(τlog⁡(τ/ε)/log⁡log⁡(τ/ε)) queries for general Lindbladians (Li and Wang 2023).

But

Requires block encoding of Hamiltonian and projected unitary encoding of stacked jump operators. Time-dependent case requires Lipschitz continuity and coherent time-indexed oracle access.

Tools

transducer framework · block encoding · projected unitary encoding · catalyst-removal error analysis · compressed Kraus-label representation

Abstract

We give a quantum algorithm for Lindbladian simulation given a block encoding of the Hamiltonian H and a projected unitary encoding of the stacked jump operator B=∑_(k=1)^m |k⟩⊗L_k, with normalization factors α_H and α_B, respectively. For evolution time t, set τ=(α_H+α_B²)t. The algorithm approximates the evolution channel to diamond-norm error ε using O (τ+(log(1/ε))/(log(e+log(1/ε)/τ))) oracle queries, matching the query lower bound for Hamiltonian simulation. The number of additional one- and two-qubit gates is linear in the query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors. The query- and gate-complexity bounds extend to Lipschitz-continuous time-dependent Lindbladians under coherent time-indexed oracle access. Our construction uses a one-query transducer that implements a product of rational approximations to short-time evolution when supplied with a catalyst. We bound the error from omitting the catalyst by exploiting orthogonality between different sequences of Kraus labels. The gate implementation combines a compressed Kraus-label representation, which stores only the positions and values of the nonzero labels, with the rotation factorization of Chen et al.

item.title: Securing quantum error correction against misleading advice from AI agents
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Passive syndrome-history distributions are exactly symmetric under coherent-rotation sign reversal RX(−heta)=RX(heta)†, but signed terminal logical calibration resolves the ambiguity to certify QEC recovery updates. An evaluator using confidence sets and drift bounds blocks 100% of tested harmful AI advice proposals under valid drift premises while accepting 60 of 96 beneficial updates with a channel-specific derivative bound.

Grade 0.360 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · A. Barics Özgüler

Figure

Distribution of all 256 one-round syndrome probabilities for the encoded calibration state at θ=±0.10 rad and the corresponding recovery infidelity. Identical syndrome distributions across signs produce opposite recovery outcomes for a fixed correction table, demonstrating why passive records cannot distinguish harmful from beneficial updates.

Asks

Can an attacker turn influence over an AI adviser into a harmful quantum error-correction recovery update?

But

Simulated evaluation assuming trusted records, evaluator, clock, and bounded noise drift rate v; violating the drift premise permits harmful updates.

Tools

odd-distance periodic square toric code · terminal logical measurement calibration · interval-bounded risk evaluator · LLM-assisted controller (Qwen3, Gemma 3, GPT-OSS)

Abstract

Can an attacker turn influence over an artificial intelligence (AI) adviser into a harmful quantum error-correction update? We identify an ambiguity in passive syndrome records that obstructs recovery selection, then show how additional calibration measurements support certified recovery updates under uncertainty and drift. In an odd-distance square toric code with error-free preparation, syndrome measurements, and recovery operations, opposite coherent X rotations produce identical passive syndrome-history distributions. Yet a fixed phase correction can help at one sign and harm at the other. A terminal logical measurement on known encoded calibration states supplies the missing sign information. A separate evaluator accepts an update only when calibration uncertainty and a justified drift bound certify improvement over the current recovery, without assuming that the adviser recommends correctly. In simulated advice attacks, calibration-confidence checks reject harmful proposals while retaining beneficial updates under honest advice. We derive sufficient limits on calibration age that require improvement through deployment. In matched simulations, a validated channel-specific bound retains more beneficial updates than the general bound after accounting for evaluation time, while preventing the tested harmful activations under the stated drift assumption. A separate surface-code experiment includes stochastic circuit faults and noise changing during acquisition. Deterministic controllers achieve at least as many beneficial updates with the same observations. Violating the drift assumption permits harmful acceptance in the toric experiment. The results identify information required for recovery selection, establish conditional guarantees against harmful updates, and quantify the recovery improvements forgone through conservative acceptance.
